extracted.intended_audience: mathematics researchers, graduate students, prospective NSF fellowship applicants, Notices contributors and readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and selection criteria for NSF Graduate Fellowship applications in mathematics (what reviewers look for, letter and statement expectations, eligibility, and ranking procedure). Also includes Notices Forum submission length guidance and program-selection principles for research programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum article length and submission
rubrics_metrics.description: The Forum section publishes short articles on issues that are of interest to the mathematical community. Articles should be between 1000 and 2500 words long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers are invited to submit articles for possible inclusion in Forum to: Notices Forum Editor, American Mathematical Society, P.O. Box 6248, Providence, RI 02940 or electronically to notices@math.ams.com.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSF evaluation components
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores and materials considered include GRE subject test scores, letters of recommendation, grades, and individual student statements; GRE scores are just one consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All of these components matter; a perfect GRE subject score is not sufficient by itself. Letters, grades, and personal statements are also very important in the holistic evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters of recommendation (content and authorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully written and appropriate letters of recommendation are extremely helpful in the evaluation process; comparisons between two or more applicants and comparisons to successful mathematicians at a similar stage are especially influential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters from scientists other than mathematicians tend to carry less weight and letters from nonscientists carry virtually no weight. Letter writers should make explicit comparisons and relate the applicant to benchmarks of success appropriate to their stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal statement quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Rambling and unfocused statements (under career goals, research experience) are detrimental. It is best to be concise and to the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists review many applications in a short time; information buried in long-winded statements will most likely be overlooked. Applicants should play to their strengths and mention all relevant experiences. Be concise and focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research experience (value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research experience is desirable but not considered essential to a successful application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many applicants have participated in NSF REU programs and some have published papers. Such experience is viewed positively but absence of research experience does not preclude success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant eligibility (who may apply)
rubrics_metrics.description: First-year graduate students may apply, as well as senior undergraduates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There were fewer first-year graduate student applicants than expected; faculty should alert eligible students (including first-year grads) to apply and help them find letter writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of diversity and separate programs
rubrics_metrics.description: The NSF encourages applications from members of minority groups, women, and persons with disabilities, although panelists are expected to disregard race, sex, and handicap in their deliberations. There is a separate program for minority fellowships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may compete in both programs where applicable. The panel noted barriers women may face and suggested interest in additional fellowship programs targeted at women, but current evaluations are not supposed to be adjusted by demographic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of 'honorable mention'
rubrics_metrics.description: In view of the large number of highly qualified candidates and the small number of fellowships, the award of 'honorable mention' should be viewed as a competitive recognition of significant achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honorable mention reflects notable merit and should be regarded positively by applicants and advisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSF ranking and selection procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The panelists present the NSF with three unordered, alphabetized lists. All the applicants in the first list and half the applicants in the second receive awards. The awardees in the second group are chosen by the National Science Foundation based on geographical and other considerations. The third list is for those who will receive honorable mention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the mechanics of how applicants are grouped and how awards/honorable mentions are ultimately decided; percentiles this year: the first two lists comprised roughly 6% and 8% of applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice to faculty regarding encouraging applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics faculties should not discourage good students from applying for an NSF Graduate Fellowship; going through the application process is beneficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encouraging students to apply yields opportunities to think about graduate school, refine goals, and gain experience writing about oneself and one’s mathematical objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: AMS fSU Small Grants focus and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Small Grants will be made directly to individuals, with a focus on graduate students, young mathematicians, and established scholars. Recommendations for grantees will be made by a panel of mathematical scientists in the former Soviet Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sloan Foundation matching funds will support this activity; the program aims to provide short-term support to stabilize and sustain mathematical research and scholarship in the former Soviet Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newton Institute program-selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The Institute will consider nearly any scientific area for a program, provided there is some serious mathematics involved and it 'ought to be an area which is going through an exciting stage' and 'it probably ought to be one which brings people together from different backgrounds, different disciplines, or makes a new contribution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Institute avoids orthodox, conventional-type meetings and prefers programs that are new, interdisciplinary, and capable of fostering collaboration and fresh developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker guidance for conference talks (accessibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plenary and many lectures were expository and accessible to a general mathematical audience; speakers were impressed upon the need to make their talks accessible with a good balance of technical details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For broad conferences, talks should be expository, reach a general mathematical audience, and balance technical depth with accessibility (some lectures even aimed to be understandable to high-school students).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference programming and outreach (ECM)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ECM included Round Tables examining relations between mathematics and society, a 'Junior Congress' for high school students, public exhibits (Horizons Mathematiques), puzzle exhibits, mathematical films, and music—efforts to reach a broader audience of nonmathematicians and young people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers planning large congresses can enhance impact by including outreach events, exhibits, and junior programs to engage students and the general public.
